written.myAnswer: Identify a problem; make observations and gather information; propose a hypothesis; test it through experiments; record and analyse results; develop a theory from the evidence; and test it repeatedly, potentially establishing a law.

A hypothesis is a proposed explanation based on observations that can be tested. For example, the hypothesis that light travels in straight lines can be tested by aligning holes in cardboard sheets and observing whether torchlight passes through them.

A theory is a logical explanation of the causes and effects of events in nature, supported by careful testing. A law describes a regular behaviour of nature that has been tested repeatedly and is generally accepted; it can be used to make predictions.

Falsifiability means that a theory makes predictions that can be tested and could potentially be shown to be false. It is important because testable, falsifiable claims can be evaluated scientifically, unlike vague or untestable claims.

A limited set of agreeing results cannot show that a prediction will always hold, since untested cases may differ. But one reliable counterexample is enough to show that the prediction is not always correct.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation, and an experiment is an organized, repeatable way to test it. Experimental results provide evidence for accepting, changing, or rejecting the hypothesis.

The scientific method is a systematic approach to investigating problems in the natural and physical world. Its main steps are identifying a problem, making observations and gathering information, proposing a testable hypothesis, testing it through experiments, recording and analysing results, and developing and repeatedly testing explanations that may lead to a law. For example, observing shadows may lead to the hypothesis that light travels in straight lines. Align holes in several cardboard sheets between a torch and an observer: light passes through when the holes are aligned and is blocked when one sheet is moved out of line. This supports the hypothesis; repeated testing can build confidence in the explanation.
